title: How the MARS Turbine Works
summary: Josh and Chuck explore the MARS turbine, a tethered, helium-filled blimp-like wind generator with spinning rotor "wings" developed by the company Magenn (the transcript renders it as "MAGEn"), which floats about a thousand feet up to harness stronger winds. They cover why bats die near conventional wind turbines (pressure drop causing lung damage rather than collisions), wind energy statistics, the environmental downsides of ground-based turbines (roads, soil erosion, habitat fragmentation), how the MARS turbine works (Magnus effect, electromagnetic induction, tethers doubling as cables), its materials (Dacron, Vectran, Tedlar, Mylar), helium leakage, wind speed tolerance and overspeed safety systems, cost per kilowatt-hour, FAA rules for tethered balloons, possible uses in remote or disaster settings, and a listener mail segment plus a South by Southwest panel-voting plug.

segments.title: Opening banter and bats vs. wind turbines
segments.summary: Hosts open with banter, then discuss white-nose fungus killing bats and the mystery of bats dying near wind turbines with no visible injury; the answer is lung damage from pressure drop near the blades.

segments.title: Wind energy statistics
segments.summary: Chuck gives worldwide wind electricity production figures for 2009, notes wind's small share of total electricity, and says capacity doubles about every three years.

segments.title: Environmental impact of ground-based turbines
segments.summary: Ground turbines are enormous; installing them requires new roads that cause soil erosion and habitat fragmentation, plus bird and bat deaths.

segments.title: How the MARS turbine works
segments.summary: Introduction of the MARS (Major Air Rotor System) from Magenn: a floating, rotating helium blimp-like craft tethered to the ground, with tethers that double as electrical cables. Generation relies on electromagnetic induction, and altitude gives stronger winds.

segments.title: Wind speed, altitude, and safety controls
segments.summary: Wind speed rises with elevation, so high altitude gives more power. The turbine produces power at about seven miles per hour and tolerates winds up to about sixty-three miles per hour, with overspeed reel-in and emergency deflation systems.

segments.title: Materials and helium leakage
segments.summary: The outer fabric is woven Dacron, fins are Vectran, the coating is Tedlar, and the interior is Mylar. Helium leaks about half a percent per month, requiring periodic top-offs; the company claims about fifteen years without major maintenance.

segments.title: Magnus effect and stability
segments.summary: The spin creates lift via the Magnus effect, which together with helium keeps the craft within forty-five degrees of vertical. The Magnus airship, invented by Freddy Ferguson, is the precursor.

segments.title: Costs and FAA rules
segments.summary: Upfront cost estimates have fallen to about four dollars and seventy cents per watt; operating cost is about fifteen cents per kilowatt-hour. FAA permits require a blinking tether and no operation within five miles of an airport or in North American flight paths. Possible uses include remote and disaster sites.

segments.title: Future models and test sites
segments.summary: A four-kilowatt backpack model is envisioned in five to ten years; the company is taking orders and seeking test locations.

segments.title: South by Southwest panel vote and listener mail
segments.summary: Hosts ask listeners to vote for their South by Southwest panel, then read listener mail about the search bar phrase and a tick-eating memory.
